cognitiveEngineeringPage.introText:
Applied cognitive engineering in AI means structuring and organizing the flow of thought of artificial intelligence.

Instead of treating a large language model as a black box where you send queries and hope for a good answer, Orazaka divides each interaction into clear, specialized stages. This guarantees data security, factual grounding, and AI predictability.
cognitiveEngineeringPage.visionText:
Traditional enterprise chatbots send your queries directly to cloud servers without intermediate checks, leading to severe data leakage and hallucination risks.

Krizaka designed Orazaka to change this. Orazaka acts as a cognitive engineering copilot: it cleans the query, fetches local memory and knowledge, applies safety checks, and validates the output locally on your machine before delivery. Total sovereignty, fully compliant with Law 25 and GDPR.

intro.title: Three clans. One fight: what's yours stays yours.
intro.lead: Krizaka began with a refusal. Your data shouldn't have to leave home to be useful. A creator shouldn't have to hand a fortune to a platform to get paid. And nobody should have to take software on faith. So we forge our own — in the open, line by line — and we named it after the legends that taught us what trust costs.

krizaka.title: The blade folded in the open
body: A kris is a blade forged in layers: iron folded onto iron, again and again, until a pattern rises in the steel. Zaka is the slope you climb, one step at a time. Krizaka is the forge halfway up that hill.

Why a forge? Because the software we were asked to trust had turned into a black box — data shipped to someone else's cloud, income routed through someone else's rules, code nobody outside could read. We set out to build the opposite, and to prove it rather than promise it.
Nothing leaves the forge unfolded, untested or undocumented, and everything that leaves it is open source under Apache-2.0. You don't have to believe us: read the pattern in the steel.

orazaka.title: The oracle that never leaves home
body: Ōrāre: to speak, to ask — the Latin root of oracle. In the old stories you climbed to the oracle with your question, and you trusted it with something private.

Today, asking an AI usually means carrying your contracts, your files and your ideas down to someone else's valley. For a lot of teams that's a deal-breaker, so they do without. We think that's the wrong trade.

Orazaka brings the oracle to your hill: answers drawn from your own documents, visuals generated on your machines, Studios that take the repeat work — on your infrastructure, under your rules. Your questions and your answers stay in the house, and every line that touches them is public, so your security team can check instead of trust.

orochia.title: Eight heads, one deal: the creator keeps 90%
body: Yamata no Orochi is the eight-headed serpent of Japan's oldest chronicles. Players of a certain age met it somewhere else too: waiting at the end of a 1990s arcade tournament, sealed by three clans and their sacred treasures.

The creator economy has a serpent of its own: heavy cuts, payouts nobody can audit, links that leak, accounts closed overnight. Creators do the work and carry the risk — and too often they're the last to be paid.

Orochia is our answer: a video platform where the creator keeps 90% of every sale, every movement is written once in a double-entry ledger, and the whole thing runs on servers you choose. In the myth, Susanoo doesn't win by force — he sets out eight vats, one for each head. Orochia sets out one answer for each.

cdn.title: Direct-to-CDN video
cdn.body: Creators upload straight to Bunny Stream (resumable Tus). Playback uses signed HLS URLs that expire after 5 minutes: video never goes through the application servers.

access.title: Server-side access control
access.body: Every play is authorised on the server against the video's own rule — public, approved followers, contacts, paid unlock (never below the creator's minimum) or invited only. No raw media URL is ever exposed.

audiences.title: Audiences the creator chooses
audiences.body: Invite people one by one or open a video to reusable, private lists — add someone and they're in, remove them and they're out. Invited-only videos are never listed. Collections get the same permissions.

engagement.title: Engagement that means something
engagement.body: Views counted once per viewer and day, never the creator's own; likes, threaded comments the creator can moderate or close, and shares — each counter moves with the record that justifies it.

payments.title: Gateway-confirmed payments
payments.body: An unlock records a payment intent, then redirects to CCBill, Segpay, NowPayments or Stripe. Access is granted only on the provider's signed webhook — exactly once, even if the webhook is replayed.

compliance.title: Built-in 18+ compliance
compliance.body: 18+ certification at sign-up, 18 U.S.C. § 2257 record checks before any upload, and content reports (suspected minors, non-consensual content, DMCA) persisted and triaged first.

auctions.title: Video auctions
auctions.body: Creators put a video up for auction; the price moves in real time for everyone watching. Bids are held in credits and released the moment they are outbid, a last-minute bid adds two minutes, and only the winner watches — or downloads — the video.

wallet.title: A wallet of credits
wallet.body: Members top up once through the gateway's hosted checkout, then tip, unlock and bid in one tap. The balance is an append-only ledger: every movement written once, refunded when a payment does not complete.

challenges.title: Challenges, funded in escrow
challenges.body: A creator's all-or-nothing goal, a dare to one creator, or an open call creators apply to. Fans pledge credits that are held until the video or story is delivered — paid then, given back otherwise. Real-time pot, leaderboard, no chargeback race.

decisions.lead: Every guarantee on this page is a decision in krizaka/orochia — what we chose, what we refused, why, and what you give up.

items.chose: Access granted only on the payment provider's signed webhook — exactly once.
items.refused: Unlocking as soon as the checkout page says "thank you".
items.because: A redirect can be forged or replayed; a signed webhook cannot.
items.cost: A few seconds between payment and playback.

items.refused: A card charge for every tip, unlock and bid.
items.because: One top-up, then one tap — and every movement written once, auditable, refundable.
items.cost: Fans top up before they spend; a balance to keep in mind.

items.cost: Links cannot be bookmarked or embedded elsewhere — by design.

items.because: Some content must never go online, not even for a minute.
items.cost: A creator's onboarding takes longer than a sign-up.

matching.title: Mutual batches, our signature
matching.lead: Most apps rank people. Yazakia asks another question: would these two choose each other?

decisions.chose: A pair is worth its weaker direction: what A looks for in B and what B looks for in A — the lower of the two, `min(A→B, B→A)`.
decisions.refused: A one-way ranking that shows you whoever fits you, whether or not you fit them.
decisions.because: That is how ghost profiles and dead-end matches are made. With the minimum, B only appears to A if A stands a chance with B.
decisions.cost: Smaller batches, sometimes none: when the pool is thin, the agent says so plainly and tells you when a batch is ready.

decisions.chose: Reasons, written in words, in both directions: “why you two”.
decisions.refused: A compatibility percentage.
decisions.because: A number invites comparing people like products; a reason invites a conversation.
decisions.cost: Every reason is written from both portraits — more work for the agent, nothing to show off.

decisions.chose: The next batch waits for your debrief.
decisions.refused: Paying to skip the debrief or to get a bigger batch — in no plan, ever.
decisions.because: The debrief is what makes the next batch better; selling a way around it would break the loop.

sections.title: Our commitment
paragraphs: Krizaka builds software that keeps data where it belongs. This page says exactly what this website collects, and nothing is hidden behind it.

sections.title: What this website collects
paragraphs: When you write to us through the contact form, we receive your name, your e-mail address, your organisation if you give it, the topic and your message. We use them only to reply to you.

The message is delivered to the team by e-mail (through our e-mail provider, Mailgun) or to our team messaging. We keep it as long as the conversation needs it, then delete it. We never sell it, share it for marketing or use it to profile you.
Our host (Vercel) keeps technical logs — IP address, time, page — for security and abuse prevention, under its own policy.

sections.title: Cookies and local storage
paragraphs: One functional cookie, NEXT_LOCALE, remembers the language you chose (one year). Your theme preference is kept in your browser's local storage.
No analytics, no advertising, no tracking scripts, no third-party cookies.

sections.title: Our software
paragraphs: Orazaka and Orochia are self-hosted: they run on your infrastructure and process data under your control. They send us no telemetry.
If you connect external services to them (AI providers, payment gateways, video CDN), the data you send goes directly to those providers under their own policies.

sections.title: Your rights
paragraphs: Under Quebec's Law 25 and the GDPR you may ask to access, correct or delete the information you sent us, or withdraw your consent. Write to us through the contact form and we will answer within 30 days.

sections.title: Contact

The software provides tools for these duties; it does not fulfil them for you.

decisions.title: What we chose, and what it costs you.
decisions.lead: Every promise above is a decision in the code. Here is what we refused, why, and the price you pay for it — said plainly.

items.chose: Local inference by default — Ollama on your machines.
items.refused: A cloud API as the default model, with "privacy mode" as an option.
items.because: A default is what 90 % of requests use: the safe path has to be the easy one.
items.cost: You need a machine that can run models (Apple Silicon, or a Linux box with a GPU).

items.chose: One governed pipeline for every request: identity, security, credits, validation.
items.refused: Checks written feature by feature, in each service.
items.because: A rule enforced in one place cannot be forgotten in the next feature.
items.cost: A few milliseconds per request, and a new capability must go through the pipeline.

items.because: A sovereign tool that reports on you is not sovereign — and you can audit that it doesn't.
items.cost: We learn from you only when you tell us: Discussions, issues, the contact form.

items.because: An approval is the cheapest audit there is.
items.cost: One more click per action — on purpose.

krizaka-platform-kit.trap: Publishing an event right after the database write: on a crash between the two, the event is lost; send it first and a rollback has already told the world. A failing `@RabbitListener` requeued forever blocks its queue. Every service invents its own error JSON. Across Orazaka's services this code existed five to seven times — with three live bugs between the copies.
krizaka-platform-kit.answer: Four modules and four starters: one security baseline for every filter chain, events through a transactional outbox, consumer queues that retry then dead-letter, idempotent consumption, RFC 9457 errors with a request id, and required service names on every metric.
krizaka-platform-kit.rule: Nothing is open by omission. `SecurityBaseline` ends every chain with `anyRequest().authenticated()`: the path you forgot to list is closed, not public.
problem: Dual write: a service that writes its row then calls `rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend` loses the event when it crashes in between, and one that sends first announces changes that roll back.
Poison messages: a listener that throws on a malformed message is redelivered at once, forever, and nothing else in the queue moves.

Deduplication done by hand: a "does it exist? then insert" lets two overlapping deliveries both through — exactly when a broker redelivers a slow first attempt — and a claim kept after a failure silently drops the retry.
Security chains copied per service: two of six had drifted in Orazaka; one answered a CORS preflight with 401.

decisions.chose: A transactional outbox: `EventPublisher.publish` writes a row of your outbox in your transaction; a relay claims rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and publishes them, with a `messageId` chosen at write time.
decisions.refused: Publishing to the broker from the service method, and a distributed transaction (XA) across database and broker.
decisions.because: The event commits or rolls back with the change. A relay that crashes republishes the same `messageId`, and the consumer's dedup makes it a no-op.
decisions.cost: An outbox table per context (you implement `OutboxStore` over your schema) and a polling delay between commit and publish.

decisions.chose: The envelope in AMQP headers (`kz-type`, `kz-version`, `kz-producer`, `kz-correlation-id`, `kz-occurred-at`), the body the bare event, and a JSON Schema per event in the producer's `-api` module.
decisions.refused: A shared jar of event DTOs, and a JSON wrapper around every body.
decisions.because: A shared DTO jar ties every service's release to every other's. A schema checked by tests on both sides (`EventContractTest`) gives the contract without the coupling, and the body stays readable by any language.
decisions.cost: Each consumer keeps its own tolerant copy of the event and one contract test.

decisions.chose: Quorum queues declared in one line (`KrizakaQueues.consumer`), a stateless retry with back-off — 5 attempts from 500 ms — then the queue’s `.dlq` twin with the original headers and the exception.
decisions.refused: Spring's default requeue on failure.
decisions.because: A requeued poison message loops forever; in the DLQ it is visible, with the reason, and can be replayed by hand.
decisions.cost: A queue already declared as classic must be drained and redeclared once.

decisions.chose: RFC 9457 Problem Details for every error: a `DomainException` becomes its 4xx with a stable code and the `requestId`; bean validation a 422 with `errors[]`; anything unexpected a 500 that never carries its message.
decisions.refused: Free-form error bodies per service, and stack traces or exception messages in 500 responses.
decisions.because: A client handles one shape, and the `requestId` in the response is the one in the log line — a support ticket points at the failure.
decisions.cost: Your exceptions extend `DomainException` (`NotFoundException`, `ConflictException`…) to choose their status.

decisions.chose: Starters that are POMs only, over modules usable alone; defaults applied at the lowest priority.
decisions.refused: Renaming the modules into starters, and defaults that override `application.yml`.
decisions.because: A product declares capabilities, not the Spring list behind them; a Spring Boot upgrade changes the starters, not your POM — and your `application.yml` always wins.
decisions.cost: Java 21 and Spring Boot 4.0 only.

notFor: Your services run on Spring Boot 3 or Java 17 — the kit targets Spring Boot 4.0 and Java 21.
Your HTTP layer is WebFlux: `krizaka-web` configures servlet applications only.
Your bus is Kafka: `krizaka-messaging` is RabbitMQ (AMQP 0-9-1) only.
Your tokens come from an external identity provider signing with RS256 or ES256: `krizaka-security` verifies HS256 today.
krizaka-platform-kit.status: 0.2.0 on Maven Central (2026-10-10): the four modules and the four starters, built and tested on real PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ in CI.

next.processOnce: `MessageDedup.processOnce` — claim, run, give the claim back on failure. Five listeners in notifications and billing repeat those eight lines today; one of them documents the forgotten release as "the settlement is lost forever". Lands in 0.3.0.
next.keys: One shared HS256 secret signs and verifies: a service that can verify can mint. Decided: issuer-signed session tokens (JWKS) and per-caller service tokens, HS256 deprecated over one minor.

krizaka-platform-kit.headline: An event published after the commit is lost on the next crash.
does: Events go through a transactional outbox: they commit or roll back with your data.
Queues retry 5 times, then dead-letter to `.dlq` — a poison message never loops.
One security baseline and RFC 9457 errors with a `requestId`, in every service.

krizaka-users.name: Users
krizaka-users.tagline: Sign-up, login, profiles, API keys and roles as a service — with a typed client for the others.
krizaka-users.trap: Sign-up looks like a weekend. Then come e-mail verification, reset tokens that must expire and be single-use, Google and GitHub accounts to link, API keys, roles in a JWT — and every other service validating that JWT its own way.
krizaka-users.answer: A Spring Boot service (or the `-core` you embed) that registers, verifies, logs in with a password or Google/GitHub, resets passwords, issues API keys and session JWTs carrying roles — and a client that every other service calls with a `SERVICE` token.
krizaka-users.rule: The owl knows every face and keeps no secret in clear: a reset token is single-use, stored as a SHA-256 hash and dead after 15 minutes; a password is a BCrypt hash; a provider key is encrypted with AES-256 before it touches the disk.
problem: Reset links that work twice, never expire, or sit in the database in clear text — readable by anyone with a backup.
A users table that grows a column per product feature until another product cannot reuse it.
Every service calling the identity service on every request — identity down means everything down.

decisions.chose: Other services verify the session JWT locally (`krizaka-security`), with roles in the token.
decisions.refused: Calling the users service (token introspection) on every request.
decisions.because: The users service being down does not take the platform down, and a request costs no network hop.
decisions.cost: A revoked session stays valid until it expires (`PT12H` by default, `IDENTITY_JWT_TTL`).

decisions.chose: A profile is a theme plus attributes your application defines — the answers of an onboarding form whose JSON schema you supply — stored as given and never interpreted.
decisions.refused: A fixed profile model with product fields.
decisions.because: The service knows users, not your product; Orazaka's own fields moved out of it into its onboarding answers.
decisions.cost: Your code reads its attributes with its own defaults.

decisions.chose: A published contract (`krizaka-users-api`), a client with a per-entry cache, and an embeddable `-core`.
decisions.refused: A library that each application wires to its own tables.
decisions.because: One place hashes passwords and signs tokens; a fix lands once.
decisions.cost: A PostgreSQL database and RabbitMQ for its events (`evt.user.registered`, `evt.password.reset`).

notFor: You already run an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Entra ID): keep it.
You need SAML, enterprise SSO or multi-factor authentication: none of them is provided.
You need a revocation that takes effect before the token expires.
krizaka-users.status: 0.1.0 on Maven Central (api, client, core). 0.2.0 — event schemas checked against their producers — is merged and ships in November.

next.release: BOM 0.2.0 manages this block at an unpublished 0.2.0: declare 0.1.0 explicitly until BOM 0.3.0.
next.keys: Session tokens signed by this service only, verified with its JWKS by the others — no shared secret.

krizaka-users.headline: Sign-up looks like a weekend. Reset tokens, OAuth and JWTs make it a quarter.
does: Register, verify, log in with a password or Google/GitHub, reset — as a service.

A typed `UserDirectoryClient` with a `SERVICE` token and a per-entry cache.

krizaka-notifications.name: Notifications
krizaka-notifications.tagline: E-mail, SMS and webhooks behind one event: applications never talk to an SMTP server again.
krizaka-notifications.trap: Each service that sends its own e-mails embeds an SMTP client, templates and retries. A provider outage becomes a bug in every one of them, and an e-mail sent inside a transaction that then rolls back cannot be unsent.
krizaka-notifications.answer: A service that consumes `evt.notification.requested` (and the users events), renders a template for the locale and delivers on the requested channel: SMTP, Twilio SMS, or an HTTP webhook.
krizaka-notifications.rule: The pigeon delivers each message once — or fails where you can see it. A channel that is not configured fails and goes to the dead-letter queue; it is never skipped in silence.
problem: A sign-up that fails because the mail server is slow.
A welcome e-mail for an account whose creation rolled back.
The same redelivered message sending the same e-mail twice.

decisions.chose: An event, published through the producer's outbox.
decisions.refused: A synchronous "send e-mail" HTTP endpoint.
decisions.because: No e-mail for a rolled-back change; an SMTP outage delays mail instead of failing sign-ups; a redelivery is sent once (deduplicated by `messageId`).
decisions.cost: RabbitMQ between your application and the service.

decisions.chose: Plain-text templates on disk, one file per template and locale, an en fallback, a directory you can point elsewhere without a rebuild.
decisions.refused: An HTML template engine, for now.
decisions.because: A template a non-developer can edit, and nothing to render that can break.
decisions.cost: Plain text only today.

decisions.chose: Webhooks only to hosts on an allow-list (empty = no webhooks).
decisions.refused: Any URL a requester sends.
decisions.because: An open webhook is a server-side request forgery waiting to happen.
decisions.cost: You declare the hosts.

notFor: You need open and click tracking, campaigns or rich HTML e-mails: use a marketing e-mail service.
Your application has no message broker and won't run one.
You need mobile push: not a channel yet (Orochia uses Expo's push service on its own).
krizaka-notifications.status: 0.1.0 on Maven Central (the `-api` contract). The service is built from source or as an image; 0.2.0 ships in November.

next.release: BOM 0.2.0 manages this block at an unpublished 0.2.0: declare 0.1.0 explicitly until BOM 0.3.0.

does: Publish `evt.notification.requested` in your transaction — no SMTP client in your service.

E-mail (SMTP), SMS (Twilio) or a webhook to allow-listed hosts: the same request.

krizaka-billing.name: Billing & credits
krizaka-billing.tagline: Credits, wallets, plans, a versioned price book and metering: hold → settle → release.
krizaka-billing.trap: Charging for expensive work goes wrong two ways: debit afterwards and the work ran on credit nobody had; debit up front and a failed job is billed. Then a "job done" message is redelivered and the same job is debited twice.
krizaka-billing.answer: A service and a typed client: a caller holds the estimated credits before expensive work, then settles the measured cost or releases the hold. Holds that are never settled expire. Plans, subscriptions, packs, wallets and usage analytics around it.
krizaka-billing.rule: The flamingo gets paid for what was done, once — and nobody pays for work that failed. A failed job releases its hold; every debit carries an idempotency key.
problem: A user who starts ten expensive jobs at once with credit for one.
A failed render billed at its estimate.

decisions.chose: Hold → settle → release, with an expiry on holds.
decisions.refused: Debit after the work, and prepay without reservation.
decisions.because: Work never starts without the credit to cover it, and failure costs nothing.
decisions.cost: One synchronous call (hold) on the request path; settle and release are off it.

decisions.chose: An append-only ledger where every debit carries an idempotency key, on top of message deduplication.
decisions.refused: Trusting deduplication alone.
decisions.because: Two independent guards: a redelivery that gets past one still debits once.
decisions.cost: The ledger only grows; corrections are new entries.

decisions.chose: Prices and the hold lifetime are rows of a versioned price book; a hold pins the version it was priced at.
decisions.refused: Prices in code or configuration.
decisions.because: Repricing never changes what an in-flight job costs, and needs no deployment.
decisions.cost: A price change is a data migration you review.

decisions.chose: A no-op adapter when `krizaka.billing.enabled` is false.
decisions.refused: `if (billingEnabled)` at every call site.
decisions.because: The same code runs metered and unmetered.
decisions.cost: None worth naming.

notFor: You need invoices, taxes or card payments: billing counts credits; collecting money is yours (a top-up credits a wallet).
Your capabilities are not AI work — today. The contract still names Orazaka's (CHAT, IMAGE, AUDIO, VIDEO, AGENT) and its measurements (tokens, GPU seconds…); see below.
krizaka-billing.status: 0.1.0 on Maven Central (api, client). 0.2.0 — the outbox implements `OutboxStore.append`, every event has its JSON Schema — is merged and ships in November.

next.vocabulary: Decided: capabilities and units become keys declared in the price book, measurements a map of quantities; Orazaka keeps its enums in Orazaka. A reusable billing block cannot speak one product's vocabulary.
next.release: BOM 0.2.0 manages this block at an unpublished 0.2.0: declare 0.1.0 explicitly until BOM 0.3.0.

krizaka-billing.headline: Debit after and the work ran on credit nobody had. Debit before and failures get billed.
does: `hold` the estimate before the work, then `settleMeasured` or `release`.
Every debit carries an idempotency key: a redelivered message is charged once.
Plans, subscriptions, packs and wallets around an append-only ledger.

krizaka-build.name: Build, BOM & test kit
krizaka-build.tagline: The parent POM, the BOM and the governance tests behind every com.krizaka artifact.
krizaka-build.trap: Every multi-repository Java organisation ends up with parent POMs that drift: a module on another Java, unpinned plugins, a POM that Maven Central rejects for a missing licence block. And a BOM that imports Spring's silently overrides the Spring Boot version you chose.
krizaka-build.answer: `krizaka-parent` (Central metadata, Java 21, formatting checked, unit and integration tests, coverage, a signed release in one command), `krizaka-bom` (the compatible set of every com.krizaka artifact) and `krizaka-test-support` (architecture rules, one PostgreSQL + RabbitMQ per test run, event contract tests).
krizaka-build.rule: A rule that judges nothing passes nothing. Every rule of the test kit fails on an empty population — a typo in a package name cannot turn a check into a green tick.
problem: Conventions in a wiki: true on the day they are written.
One Testcontainers setup per repository, each starting its own database per test class.
A minor release that breaks binary compatibility, discovered by the people who upgraded.

decisions.chose: A BOM that carries only com.krizaka artifacts; the parent has no `dependencyManagement` of its own.
decisions.refused: Importing `spring-boot-dependencies` in our BOM.
decisions.because: Importing `krizaka-bom` must never pin a version you chose. Your Spring Boot BOM stays yours; ours sits beside it.
decisions.cost: You import Spring Boot's BOM (or parent) yourself.

decisions.chose: Architecture rules as tests (`CodeRules`, `SourceRules`, `ConfigBindingRules`: layering, constructor injection, private state, no Environment injection…).
decisions.refused: A review checklist.
decisions.because: A rule that runs on every build is the only kind still true six months later.
decisions.cost: Rules are opinionated: take the ones that fit, call them from your own test.

decisions.chose: japicmp in the release profile: a binary break in a minor fails the release; publication on Central confirmed by hand.
decisions.refused: SemVer by good intentions, and automatic publication.
decisions.because: A release on Central can never be deleted: a break shipped is a break forever.
decisions.cost: A deliberate break is declared in the repository for that release.

notFor: You do not publish to Maven Central and don't want our conventions (google-java-format, Java 21) on your build: import the BOM, skip the parent.
You are on Java 17 or earlier.

next.bom: BOM 0.2.0 names users, notifications and billing at a 0.2.0 that is not published yet. Decided: a BOM release resolves every artifact it manages before it is signed; BOM 0.3.0 waits for the three.

krizaka-build.headline: Parent POMs drift — and a Spring BOM silently overrides the Boot version you chose.
does: `krizaka-parent`: Java 21, pinned plugins, Central metadata, a signed release in one command.
`krizaka-bom`: the compatible set of every `com.krizaka` artifact, and nothing else.
`krizaka-test-support`: architecture rules, real PostgreSQL + RabbitMQ, event contract tests.

krizaka-ui.name: Krizaka UI
krizaka-ui.tagline: Tokens, a Tailwind v4 preset, accessible primitives, icons and i18n — web and React Native.
krizaka-ui.trap: Three products, three token vocabularies: we measured 1,153 `light:` overrides in one application, the same card written five times, and focus traps, keyboard handling and ARIA rewritten by hand in each kit.
krizaka-ui.answer: One semantic vocabulary (`--kz-*`) compiled from design tokens, a preset that turns it into Tailwind utilities, and primitives — button, card, dialog, field, tabs, toast, command palette… — with React Native parity, one entry point each. The documentation of every component is generated from its code.
krizaka-ui.rule: The owl reads the code, not a wiki: every component's page on krizaka.com/docs/ui is generated from its `meta.ts` and its named examples, and the registry tests fail when one is missing.
problem: A theme implemented as `light:` and dark: variants in every component — a new theme means touching all of them.
Accessibility rewritten per product, and wrong in at least one.
A documentation site that describes last quarter's props.

decisions.chose: One token vocabulary; dark on `:root`, light on `html.light`; a brand overrides values (`brands/scoped.css`).
decisions.refused: `light:/dark:` variants in components, and a token set per product.
decisions.because: A theme or a brand is a set of values: Orazaka's orange and Orochia's violet use the same components as this site.
decisions.cost: Components read `var(--kz-*)` only; raw palette colours are refused by the lint rules.

decisions.chose: Radix for every non-trivial interaction, variants with tailwind-variants, every story audited by axe in dark and light on each pull request.
decisions.refused: Hand-written focus traps and keyboard handling.
decisions.because: Accessibility is written once and tested where it is written.
decisions.cost: Radix in your bundle; size-limit budgets per entry keep it in check.

decisions.chose: Words arrive as props; no translation function inside the library.
decisions.refused: Bundling a translation runtime.
decisions.because: Any i18n works — ours (`@krizaka/i18n`, typed catalogues and a CI check) or yours.
decisions.cost: You pass the labels.

decisions.chose: A ratchet: per-repository counters of raw palette classes, `light:` variants, `[var(--…)]` utilities and className templates that may only go down.
decisions.refused: A big-bang migration, and a lint rule switched on at once.
decisions.because: An existing application adopts it screen by screen without letting the debt grow back.
decisions.cost: A `lint-ratchet.json` to commit and a check in CI.

notFor: You don't use Tailwind v4: the preset requires it (the tokens alone are plain CSS variables).
You want an unstyled kit and own every pixel: use Radix directly.
You need charts today: `@krizaka/charts` is being built.
krizaka-ui.status: @krizaka/ui, tokens and tailwind 2.2.0 on npm (latest) — 2.2.0 brought the five birds of this page (`@krizaka/ui/mascots`); icons, i18n, intl and config 0.1.0. Supported: majors N and N-1, fixes for six months after N+1.

next.charts: `@krizaka/charts` — theme- and brand-aware charts on Apache ECharts, each with an accessible data table, and the effects and blocks after it: the roadmap is an open epic.

krizaka-ui.headline: Three products, three token vocabularies, 1,153 `light:` overrides in one app.
does: One semantic vocabulary, `--kz-*`, compiled from design tokens — dark and light alike.
Accessible primitives with React Native parity, one entry point each.
Every component's documentation generated from its code.

principles.title: Sovereign
principles.desc: Everything runs on your infrastructure. No data is sent to a third-party cloud — Law 25 & GDPR compliant.

principles.title: Deterministic
principles.desc: No black box: each request follows an explicit, reproducible, auditable order of interceptors.

principles.title: Modular
principles.desc: A hexagonal architecture: every responsibility — security, memory, media — is a swappable module.

steps.title: Presentation
steps.what: You ask from the web client, the mobile app, the CLI or the admin console.
steps.why: Four front doors, a single engine behind them.

steps.title: Entry Gate
steps.what: The edge receives every request, exchanges an API key for a session token, and routes by path: identity, billing and studio to their services, everything else to the conversation service.
steps.why: One controlled entry point: nothing reaches a model directly.

steps.title: Security & Logic
steps.what: Before any compute, the session token is checked (stateless JWT, krizaka-security) and the entitlement interceptor verifies what you may do and can afford.
steps.why: Security and governance happen before inference — not after.

steps.title: Cognitive Engine
steps.what: The stateless hexagonal core orchestrates the request and coordinates the data flow.
steps.why: The conductor: reproducible on every single call.

steps.title: Workers & Pipeline
steps.what: The turn goes through {core} non-bypassable interceptors, then {configured} configured ones (memory, MCP, tools…); long jobs travel over RabbitMQ to the job service and the media worker.
steps.why: This is where “cognition” is assembled, one ordered step after another.

steps.title: Persistence
steps.what: Sessions, vector memory (pgvector) and identities are stored in your own databases.
steps.why: Your data stays home, from the first byte to the last.
